findings.title: Do not execute an unpinned remote script as root
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN fetches https://example.com/install.sh and pipes the response body to sh. The Dockerfile has no USER, so Docker runs that shell as root and commits the layer. There is no checksum, signature, or pinned revision, and -L will follow redirects to whatever host answers. A fetch of that URL returns the Example Domain HTML documentation page, not an installer, so the build executes that document as a shell script: the image build fails while parsing markup, and any later change of the response body runs with root and is baked into the image.

findings.title: Fail the image build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: curl's failure status is discarded. The shell form is /bin/sh -c with pipefail left off, and -s suppresses curl's error text. On a transport failure (DNS, timeout, connection reset) curl exits non-zero and writes no stdout; sh reads EOF and exits 0. Docker commits the layer and continues through COPY and CMD, so a missed install is indistinguishable from a successful one and ships as a normal image.

findings.title: Fail the image build on the install.sh HTML body
findings.whyItBreaks: https://example.com/install.sh returns HTTP 404 with a text/html body (the Example Domain page, starting with <!doctype html>). curl -sL is missing --fail, so curl exits 0 and writes that document into the pipe. There is no SHELL instruction, so pipefail is off and sh parses the HTML. A POSIX sh rejects it at parse time (dash: exit 2, Syntax error: redirection unexpected). Docker marks this RUN failed, and the image does not build.

findings.title: Do not execute an unpinned remote script as root
findings.whyItBreaks: The shell-form RUN runs as root: the Dockerfile never sets USER. curl -L follows redirects and the response body is executed by sh with no checksum or signature. Today that body is the example.com 404 page; any change or redirect at that URL becomes root commands during the build and in later layers.

findings.title: Fail the build when curl cannot download the script
findings.whyItBreaks: curl's failure is discarded: -s hides its error text, --fail is absent, and with no pipefail the pipeline status is only sh's. A transport failure writes no stdout, and sh on empty stdin exits 0 (measured on /bin/sh). Docker then commits the layer and continues at COPY/CMD, so a missed download is indistinguishable from a finished install.

findings.title: Reject the 404 HTML body piped into the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: curl -sL is missing --fail, so https://example.com/install.sh returns HTTP 404 with curl exit 0 and writes the Example Domain HTML page to stdout. That body is not a shell script: sh -n exits 2 with 'Syntax error: redirection unexpected'. Docker RUN uses /bin/sh -c and there is no SHELL override, so a reachable host fails the image build at this step.

findings.title: Fail the build when curl cannot fetch the installer
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline status is sh, and pipefail is off. busybox ash '(exit 7) | sh' exits 0, and an empty stdin makes sh exit 0. curl -s also hides the error text. On DNS, connect, or TLS failure curl writes no stdout, sh sees EOF, and Docker commits the layer as success with the install skipped.

findings.title: Surface Load errors instead of returning a blank string
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", nil) when the key is present and the stored value is empty (src/store.go:8-12) and ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent (src/store.go:9-10). LoadOrDefault ignores that error and returns the string. The exported function therefore yields "" for both a real empty entry and a failed lookup, so every caller must treat a missing key as stored data.

findings.title: Propagate or default explicitly; do not hide ErrMissing
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present and empty (src/store.go:8-12). LoadOrDefault drops that error with `_` and returns v, so every caller of this exported function receives "" for both a missing key and a stored empty string and cannot tell failure from a real value.

findings.title: Propagate Load errors from LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault discards that error and returns only the string, so every caller must treat a failed lookup as a real empty value.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run schedules one goroutine per job and returns as soon as the loop ends. No WaitGroup, channel close, or other join orders those goroutines before return, so results <- j*2 still runs after the caller continues. The usual producer pattern (call Run, then close(results), then range) races the in-flight sends and panics with send on a closed channel. A caller that reads a buffered channel immediately after Run can observe fewer than len(jobs) values. If the receiver stops, each blocked send leaves a goroutine alive for the process lifetime. ctx is never read, so cancel does not stop those sends.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run schedules one goroutine per job and returns as soon as the loop finishes, while each goroutine executes results <- j*2 only later. Previously every send finished on the caller goroutine before Run returned. A caller that closes results after Run returns (the way to end a range, since Run never closes the channel) panics with send on closed channel. A caller that returns from main or a handler when Run returns can exit or drop the channel while sends are still in flight, so doubled values disappear. The goroutines block on that send and never select on ctx.Done(), so a cancelled context leaks one blocked goroutine per job that has not been received. Sends are also unordered relative to jobs.

findings.title: Join worker goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run used to send every results value on the caller goroutine before returning, so return happened-before the caller continued. It now starts a goroutine per job at src/worker.go:7-9 and returns as soon as the loop has scheduled them, with no WaitGroup, done channel, or other join. results is caller-owned, so the previously safe pattern — close it after Run and range — races the in-flight sends and panics with send on closed channel. A read of the channel as soon as Run returns can also see a short or empty result set. The goroutines never select on ctx.Done(), so cancel does not stop those sends.

findings.title: Restore same-tenant admin requirement for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Deletion was allowed only when the session is an admin of the record's tenant (isAdmin && tenantId match). The operator is now ||, so the exported check returns true when isAdmin is false and tenantId matches (any tenant member; ownerId is never consulted) and when isAdmin is true and tenantId does not match (cross-tenant delete). Both inputs returned false before this change, and this function is the authorization decision.

findings.title: Restore admin-and-same-tenant check for delete
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported gate used to require both session.isAdmin and a matching tenantId. With ||, a non-admin whose tenantId equals record.tenantId now gets true (isAdmin is ignored on a tenant match), and an admin whose tenantId differs now gets true (the tenant check is ignored when isAdmin is true). Base denied both: {isAdmin:false, tenantId:'t1'} + record tenant 't1' was false and is now true; {isAdmin:true, tenantId:'t1'} + record tenant 't2' was false and is now true. That is same-tenant privilege escalation and a cross-tenant delete bypass on the public authorization result.

findings.title: Require admin and same tenant to delete
findings.whyItBreaks: The gate changed from conjunction to disjunction. session.isAdmin alone now returns true, so a tenant-scoped admin (isAdmin lives on Session next to tenantId; there is no super-admin flag) can delete another tenant's record. Independently, session.tenantId === record.tenantId alone returns true, so any non-admin member can delete every record in the tenant. Base denied both. Outsiders (non-admin, other tenant) are still denied, and the legitimate admin-of-same-tenant case stays allowed, so this is a pure authorization widening on the exported delete decision.

findings.title: Propagate parse failures instead of persisting defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch on exported parseSettings discards JSON.parse SyntaxError and the thrown "bad theme" / "bad fontSize" errors and returns {theme:"light", fontSize:14}. Those failures used to propagate. updateFontSize has no try/catch: it assigns the requested size and save() writes the object. A payload with a valid theme and an invalid fontSize, such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}, or any malformed JSON, previously left storage unchanged; it now persists {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}. Callers cannot tell a real light/14 config from a failed parse, so the write path treats failure as user settings.

findings.title: Propagate parseSettings errors instead of returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: parseSettings is exported and used to throw on invalid JSON, a non-string theme, or a non-number fontSize. The new catch returns { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 } for every failure, which is indistinguishable from a real config that is already the defaults. updateFontSize (line 20) treats that value as a successful parse, overwrites fontSize, and save() writes it. For raw {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"large"} the old path threw "bad fontSize" before save and left storage unchanged; the new path saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>} and deletes theme "dark". The same overwrite happens for corrupt JSON.

findings.title: Propagate parseSettings errors instead of saving defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch discards JSON.parse failures and the thrown "bad theme" / "bad fontSize" errors and returns {theme:"light", fontSize:14}. updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) treats that object as a successful parse, then save() at line 22 writes it. A stored document such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"} previously threw on the fontSize check and never reached save, leaving the dark theme intact; it now persists {"theme":"light","fontSize":<requested size>}. The same path overwrites storage when raw is not JSON at all. Because parseSettings is exported and always returns Settings, callers cannot tell a real light/14 config from a failed parse.

findings.title: Return branch artifacts instead of the verified ref
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport(build, branch) sets builtFrom to build.ref(branch) but now sets artifacts to build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). For any branch whose ref is not "verified", the report lists another commit's artifacts while claiming they were built from the requested branch. Callers that publish or gate on that pair ship or attest the wrong artifacts.

findings.title: Load report artifacts from the same commit as builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom to build.ref(branch), then resolves a second ref with the literal name "verified" and passes that commit to artifactsAt. For a caller that passes branch "main", the returned report has builtFrom = ref("main") and artifacts = artifactsAt(ref("verified")). Build.ref maps a ref name to a commit, so those two names yield different commits, and the report attributes the verified ref's artifacts to the branch commit. The branch argument no longer selects the artifact set.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom to build.ref(branch) but now passes build.ref("verified") to artifactsAt. For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", the returned artifacts belong to the verified ref while builtFrom names the branch commit, so callers publish or deploy the wrong artifact set under that commit. The branch argument no longer selects artifacts.

findings.title: Cap recentEntries to limit instead of returning every row
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc on recentEntries promises at most `limit` newest entries, and the previous body did `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new body reverses a copy and, for every limit > 0, returns that entire copy. renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20) and then copies page.length items into a 20-slot array (src/feed.ts:9-11). When all.length > 20 the page is the full reversed list, the loop extends out past index 19, and the rendered feed is the entire history instead of the 20 newest entries.

findings.title: Cap recentEntries to the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported doc promises at most `limit` newest entries. For limit > 0 the body returns the entire reversed copy, so length is all.length. renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20), allocates a 20-element array, and assigns page[i] for every i < page.length. When all.length > 20, that loop extends the array and renderFeed returns the whole history.

findings.title: Cap recentEntries at limit instead of returning every row
findings.whyItBreaks: The unchanged doc promises at most `limit` entries, newest first, and the previous body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. For every limit > 0 the new body returns the entire reversed copy. renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20) and then assigns page[i] for i < page.length into an array allocated at length 20. When all.length > 20, page.length exceeds 20, those assignments extend out, and the rendered feed is the full reversed history. The same uncapped list is what any caller of the exported function receives for a positive limit.

findings.title: Count only rendered rows in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now builds rows from entries where stale is false, but headerLines still receives entries.length and writes `# entry-count: N`. Whenever any entry is stale, N is larger than the number of path/size lines. A reader that trusts the header over-reads or rejects the manifest. The mismatch is the case this change exists to handle; with every entry live the old count still matches.

findings.title: Fix entry-count to match filtered manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now emits rows only for entries with stale=false, but headerLines still receives entries.length. # entry-count is interpolated verbatim from that argument, so any stale input makes the published count larger than the number of data rows. One live entry and one stale entry yields `# entry-count: 2` followed by a single row; a reader that trusts the header will expect another row that is not in the document. Before this change every entry was a row, so entries.length matched the body.

findings.title: Align entry-count with rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now emits a row only for entries with stale=false, but headerLines still receives entries.length. # entry-count previously equaled the number of data rows because every entry was mapped into a row. With one live and one stale entry the document is `# entry-count: 2` followed by a single path/size row, so any reader that trusts the header to size, verify, or consume N entries treats a short body as a complete manifest.

findings.title: Return False when stored_hash is not an ASCII string
findings.whyItBreaks: token_hash() returns an ASCII str. hmac.compare_digest on Python 3.12 raises TypeError when stored_hash is None, bytes, or a non-ASCII str (verified: TypeError versus == returning False). guard is the only caller and uses `if not check(...)` at app/token.py:14 to return {"status": 401}. The TypeError is uncaught, so those stored hashes escape guard and the request never gets the 401 response. A matching ASCII hex digest still compares equal and still runs the handler.

findings.title: Do not reject viewers in the shared eligibility gate
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible is the only gate in handle. Previously an active viewer with attempts < 5 passed it and handle returned "read-only" (src/handler.ts:25). The new req.role === "viewer" guard returns false for every viewer, so handle takes the reject branch at src/handler.ts:24 and the read-only outcome is unreachable. Read-only is a legitimate result of this gate, independent of the attempt cap; admins still reach "elevated" and editors still reach "processed".

findings.title: Remove the viewer gate that blocks the read-only route
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible is the only proceed/reject gate, and handle is its only caller. The new req.role === "viewer" check returns false for every viewer, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 and never reaches the viewer branch at line 25. An active viewer with attempts under MAX_ATTEMPTS (5) previously received "read-only" and now receives "rejected". Viewer routing is handle's own concern; this predicate does not legitimately govern that action.

findings.title: Stop rejecting active viewers before read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false for every viewer. Its only caller, handle, returns "rejected" before the viewer branch, so an active viewer with attempts < 5 gets "rejected" instead of "read-only". That read-only outcome is unreachable.

findings.title: Do not block saveDraft when payment is missing
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by submitOrder and saveDraft. Adding order.payment === "paid" makes saveDraft({state:"draft", payment:"missing"}) take the !canProceed branch and return "blocked" instead of "saved". An unpaid draft is a valid Order and saving it does not depend on payment; that check only legitimately governs submit.

findings.title: Do not block unpaid draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now requires payment === "paid" in addition to state !== "ready". saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) uses that same predicate, so {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} returns "blocked". Previously state !== "ready" was true and saveDraft returned "saved". Payment status does not govern saving a draft; "missing" is a valid unpaid draft. submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) is a distinct action that this payment check does legitimately govern.

Callers that publish snapshot.files as the contents of snapshot.commit deploy the wrong tree, and the return value stays successful so the mismatch is invisible.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument in build()

The loop always uses max_count = 10 (src/builder.py:2-4), so build('p', limit=2) returns 10 strings and build('p', limit=100) still returns 10. Default calls match the old length only because the unused default is also 10.

The body never reads limit: max_count stays hardcoded at 10 and range(max_count) always appends 10 strings. build('p', limit=3) and build('p', 3) therefore return 10 items. Default limit=10 matches the old length only when the argument is omitted, so any non-default limit is silently ignored.

findings.title: Prevent overlapping reserves from overselling a SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve captures remaining, then awaits store.save before stock.set. await always yields, so a second reserve started before the first continuation (Promise.all or any back-to-back call) still sees the old count, passes the remaining <= 0 check, and both return true. With load(sku, 1) both calls save(sku, 0) and set 0: two successful reserves of one unit. With load(sku, 2) both save 1 and set 1, so one decrement is lost in memory and in the store. The previous synchronous reserve updated the Map before returning, so this interleaving could not happen.

findings.title: Claim stock before await so concurrent reserves cannot oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve used to check and decrement with no yield, so on the JS event loop a second call could not observe the pre-decrement count. The new await this.store.save(sku, remaining - 1) suspends before this.stock.set, including when save returns an already-resolved promise. Two overlapping reserve calls (for example Promise.all on the last unit) both read the same remaining, both pass remaining <= 0, both persist remaining - 1, and both return true, so one unit is sold twice while the map only drops by one. The same post-await stock.set writes that stale absolute snapshot, so a load() that runs during save is overwritten and an older save that settles after a newer one can persist a higher count than memory.

findings.title: Prevent overlapping reserve from overselling one unit
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve captures remaining, awaits store.save(sku, remaining-1), and only then stock.set(sku, remaining-1). The await yields before the map write, so a second reserve for the same sku reads the pre-decrement count. With load(sku, 1), both calls see 1, both pass the remaining<=0 check, both persist 0, both set 0, and both return true, so one unit is reserved twice. With load(sku, N), both persist and store N-1, so one decrement is lost. The same window lets load(sku, count) during the await get overwritten by the stale stock.set.

findings.title: Fix retry still treating millisecond backoff as seconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from seconds capped at 30 to milliseconds capped at 30_000 (2**attempt*1000). schedulePoll now passes that value straight to setTimeout, which preserves the old delays (attempt 0 = 1000ms, attempt >= 5 = 30000ms). retry still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), and sleep() already takes milliseconds via setTimeout. A failed attempt 0 now waits 1_000_000ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1_000ms, and the cap waits 30_000_000ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30_000ms, so any throwing fn stalls the retry loop by 1000× before the error is rethrown.

findings.title: Drop extra *1000 now that backoff returns milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff used to return seconds capped at 30 (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)); schedulePoll was updated to pass that value straight to setTimeout, so the helper now returns milliseconds capped at 30000. src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still does sleep(backoff(a)*1000), and sleep() feeds setTimeout in milliseconds. Attempt 0 therefore waits 1_000_000ms instead of 1_000ms, and attempt >= 5 waits 30_000_000ms (~8.3h) instead of 30_000ms. Every failed attempt in the exported retry() path stalls for 1000× the previous delay.

findings.title: Stop scaling millisecond backoff by 1000 in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() used to return seconds (cap 30) and both timers scaled by 1000. It now returns milliseconds (cap 30_000). schedulePoll passes that value straight to setTimeout, but retry() still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000) and sleep() treats its argument as milliseconds (setTimeout). Attempt 0 now waits 1_000_000ms instead of 1_000ms; attempt >= 5 waits 30_000_000ms (~8.3h) instead of 30_000ms, so each failed try stalls for the inflated delay before the next attempt or the rethrow.

findings.title: Propagate f.Close error on Save's success path
findings.whyItBreaks: On the success path Save previously returned the error from f.Close() (base store/save.go:24). defer f.Close() discards that error, and return w.Flush() yields nil whenever the buffer flush succeeds. Close runs after Flush (return operand is evaluated before defers) but its error is ignored, so a post-flush close failure (EIO, NFS commit, quota) is indistinguishable from a successful save. Save is exported; every caller is forced to treat that failure as success. Write and flush errors are still returned; only the close error was dropped.

findings.title: Propagate Save's Close error to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Save is exported. On the flush-success path, base store/save.go:24 returned the error from f.Close(). Head store/save.go:13 does defer f.Close(), which discards that error, and store/save.go:20 returns only w.Flush(). When Flush succeeds and Close fails, every caller receives nil and treats the save as successful. close(2) is where delayed write failures (for example NFS EIO) are reported, so a failed commit is indistinguishable from a completed save. Flush still runs before the deferred Close, so the buffered data is written; the lost signal is the Close error.

findings.title: Propagate File.Close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: Save is exported and its only success signal is a nil error. On the success path the previous code returned f.Close() (base store/save.go:24). The new code does defer f.Close() and return w.Flush(). Return operands run before defers, so Flush still happens before Close, but Close's error is discarded. When Flush returns nil and Close returns an error (the failure close(2) can surface for an earlier write, including EIO), Save returns nil. Callers must treat that as a completed save. Write and Flush failures are still returned; only the success-path Close error is newly swallowed. There is no in-repo caller, and every caller of this public function is forced to conflate that failure with success.

findings.title: Include the last row of each page window

The new loop uses range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is never copied. For rows [a,b,c,d,e] and page_size 3, page 0 returns [a,b] instead of [a,b,c] and page 1 returns [d] instead of [d,e]. A one-row page has end = start + 1, so range(start, start) is empty. render_page (line 40) numbers only that short list, and summarize (line 52) joins those short pages, so the last row of every page is missing from the rendered text and a one-row page becomes a blank section.

A one-row page (end == start + 1) becomes []. For rows ['a','b','c'] and page_size 2, page 0 yields ['a'] and page 1 yields []. render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) therefore emit that truncated window, silently omitting the last row of every page.

findings.title: Stop dropping the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) (lib/pagination.py:17-21), and the previous loop was range(start, end). range(start, end - 1) stops one index early, so page_window omits the last row of every page. A one-row page (start, end) = (i, i+1) becomes range(i, i) and returns []. render_page (lib/pagination.py:40-44) numbers only that truncated window, and summarize (lib/pagination.py:51-53) joins those pages, so rows disappear from the public output. Example: page_window(['a','b','c'], 0, 2) returns ['a'] and page_window(['a','b','c'], 1, 2) returns [] instead of ['a','b'] and ['c']. findings.title: Restore the TTL check so fresh entries are returned
findings.whyItBreaks: TtlCache.get returns entry.value only when Date.now() - entry.storedAt is already greater than ttlMs. Every younger entry falls through to this.entries.delete(key) and returns null. A read inside the TTL therefore evicts a live key and misses, while a read after the TTL returns the stale value and leaves it stored. Age equal to ttlMs still deletes, so only the two strict sides are swapped.

findings.title: Remove done jobs without splicing during forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach captures the length once and then increments the index after each callback. splice(index, 1) shifts the next job into the index just visited, so that job is never inspected. [{id:'a',done:true},{id:'b',done:true},{id:'c',done:false}] finishes as [{id:'b',done:true},{id:'c',done:false}]. The caller's array is mutated in place, so the leftover done job remains in the list the caller passed.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison so fresh entries hit
findings.whyItBreaks: get() used to return the value when age < ttlMs and delete it otherwise. The operator is now >, so an unexpired entry (age <= ttlMs) falls through, is deleted at line 21, and returns null, while an expired entry (age > ttlMs) is returned at line 19 and kept. A just-written key misses, and a key read after the TTL is served forever.

findings.title: Remove done jobs without skipping the next index
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach fixes len up front and then visits k, k+1, .... splice(index, 1) shifts the next job into index, and the loop then advances to index+1, so that job is never seen. pruneDone([{done:true},{done:true}]) returns [{done:true}]; any adjacent done pair leaves the later done job in the array. The same loop also mutates the caller's array and returns it, so the partial removal is visible on the input the previous filter left unchanged.

findings.title: Return fresh cache entries and expire stale ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The hit test flipped from age < ttlMs to age > ttlMs. A live entry (Date.now() - storedAt < ttlMs) falls through, is deleted at line 21, and get returns null. An expired entry (age > ttlMs) is returned and left in the map, so later gets keep serving that stale value. Age === ttlMs still expires, same as before; both strict sides are reversed. TtlCache.get is exported, so callers receive the inverted result.

findings.title: Remove every done job without skipping or mutating
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach walks a fixed increasing index while splice shifts the tail left, so the job that slides into the removed slot is never visited. pruneDone([{id:'a',done:true},{id:'b',done:true},{id:'c',done:false}]) returns [{id:'b',done:true},{id:'c',done:false}]. [done, done] likewise keeps one done job. The caller's array is mutated and returned by reference; the previous filter returned a new array and left the input intact. pruneDone is exported, so that incomplete list is the public result.

findings.title: Stop busiest from sorting the caller’s array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort reorders its receiver and returns that same array. busiest now calls rows.sort, so a caller that keeps using the array afterward sees it permanently reordered by amount descending. A frozen or sealed array, which the previous shallow copy accepted, throws TypeError on the in-place sort. The returned row is still the highest-amount element, but the caller’s collection order is lost on every non-trivial call.

findings.title: Return 0 from averageAmount when rows is empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard was removed. reduce on [] with an initial value of 0 yields 0, then line 8 divides by rows.length (0). In JavaScript 0/0 is NaN, so averageAmount([]) returns NaN. The previous function returned 0 for that input. NaN fails Number.isFinite, fails equality with 0, and JSON.stringify turns it into null, so any caller that displays, sums, or persists the result treats “no rows” as a poisoned number.

findings.title: Return 0 from averageAmount when rows is empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard that returned 0 was removed. For rows = [], reduce yields its initial value 0 and line 8 divides by rows.length, so averageAmount([]) evaluates 0/0 and returns NaN. Callers that previously received numeric zero now get a result that fails equality checks and poisons later arithmetic.

findings.title: Stop busiest from sorting the caller array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort reorders its receiver and returns that same array. The previous shallow copy was removed, so busiest now rewrites the caller's row order to amount-descending. The returned row is still the maximum, but any later read of the same array sees the ranked order instead of the order the caller passed in.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input guard in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array return of 0 was removed. For rows=[], reduce yields the initial 0 and total / rows.length evaluates to 0/0, which is NaN. Callers previously received a usable 0; NaN now fails equality checks and poisons any later arithmetic. Non-empty inputs are unchanged.

findings.title: Copy rows before sorting in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort reorders its receiver and returns that same array. Dropping the `[...rows]` copy makes busiest permanently reorder the caller's array by amount descending. The returned row is still the max (or null when empty), but any later read of the same array sees the mutated order. The previous copy left the caller array unchanged.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score order
findings.whyItBreaks: rankScores replaced the numeric comparator (b - a) with scores.sort() plus reverse(). Array.prototype.sort with no compare function orders by UTF-16 string value, not by number. For scores [2, 10, 20] the array becomes [20, 2, 10]. topPlayers then sets cutoff to scores[min(n, length) - 1]; with n = 2 that cutoff is 2 instead of 10. players.filter(score >= 2).slice(0, 2) therefore returns the score-2 and score-10 players and drops the score-20 player. formatBoard (line 20) prints that wrong list. The same inversion happens for any scores whose decimal representations are not in the same order as their numeric values (9 vs 10, 99 vs 100, negatives, decimals).

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before taking the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: rankScores replaced the numeric comparator `(a, b) => b - a` with `scores.sort(); scores.reverse()`. Default sort orders by ToString (UTF-16), not by number, and reverse keeps that order. topPlayers then treats index min(n, length)-1 as the nth-highest score. For [{name:"ann",score:9},{name:"bob",score:10}] and n=1, sort yields [10,9] because "10"<"9", reverse yields [9,10], cutoff is 9, and slice(0,1) returns ann. For n=2 the cutoff is 10, so ann (a real top-2 score) is dropped. formatBoard prints that result.

findings.title: Sort leaderboard scores numerically descending
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator orders by UTF-16 string order, and reverse() keeps that order. topPlayers then uses index min(n, length)-1 as a numeric cutoff (line 15) and keeps players with score >= cutoff (line 16). For [{score:9},{score:100}] and n=1, rankScores returns [9, 100], the cutoff is 9, and slice(0, 1) returns the score-9 player. formatBoard (line 20) prints that player as #1. The previous comparator (a, b) => b - a ranked these as [100, 9] and selected 100. Any scores with different digit lengths (or negatives) mis-rank the same way; for [2, 10, 3] and n=2 the cutoff becomes 2, so slice keeps 2 and 10 and drops 3.

findings.title: Restore constant-time compare for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the only gate in handle() (line 14): a true result runs processor(payload), a false result returns 401. signature_of() still returns the HMAC-SHA256 hex digest, but the comparison is now str equality. CPython compares strings until the first differing character, so the time to reject a guess tracks the matching prefix of the expected digest. An attacker who can observe that latency can recover signature_of(payload, secret) and then pass verify, which authorizes the processor. hmac.compare_digest was the constant-time check this path used before; hmac is still imported and still implements that API.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC compare in verify
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() runs processor(payload) only when verify() is true (app/webhook.py:14) and otherwise returns 401. verify() now decides that with str ==. CPython implements str equality as a length check plus memcmp, which returns at the first differing byte, so two wrong 64-character guesses that both take the 401 path still differ in time by how much of the SHA-256 HMAC hex digest they matched. An attacker can recover the digest prefix-by-prefix and then pass the gate. The previous hmac.compare_digest call scanned the full digest without a content-dependent early exit. The same == also accepts a non-str given_signature whose __eq__ returns True, because str equality returns NotImplemented and defers to the other operand; handle() then returns 200 and calls processor. compare_digest raised TypeError on that input and did not run the processor.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook verify
findings.whyItBreaks: signature_of() returns a SHA-256 hex digest string. Python == walks that string and returns on the first mismatched character, so verify()/handle() latency tracks how long a guess matches the expected MAC. An attacker who can time equal-length (64 hex char) guesses can recover the digest for a chosen payload, then pass the gate at handle() line 14 and have processor run on a forged body. hmac.compare_digest was the constant-time check on this path.

findings.title: Move balance updates back inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs ran inside one db.transaction() block, so any failure rolled all three back. _apply_balances now runs only after that with-block exits, which commits the ledger row first. A crash or error on the debit UPDATE leaves a posted transfer with unchanged balances; a failure on the credit UPDATE (the two UPDATEs are not in a transaction with each other either) debits the source and never credits the destination. The exception still propagates, so a retry inserts a second ledger row against already-mutated balances.

findings.title: Move balance updates back inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: with db.transaction() now wraps only _record_ledger. Leaving that block commits the ledger INSERT, and _apply_balances then runs the debit and the credit as later statements. If the credit UPDATE raises, the connection drops, or the process stops after the debit, the ledger row remains, the source balance is already reduced, and the destination balance is unchanged.

findings.title: Move balance updates back inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: with db.transaction() now wraps only _record_ledger. On block exit that INSERT is committed, and _apply_balances then runs the debit and the credit as later statements, outside that transaction and outside any shared transaction with each other. A crash, a failed credit UPDATE, or an interleaved transfer leaves a durable ledger row whose balances are missing, one-sided, or mixed with another transfer. On the base revision all three statements shared one transaction and rolled back together.

findings.title: Restore UTC calendar fields in billingDay
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously formatted the UTC date (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate). It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which follow the process timezone. At 2026-01-15T00:30:00.000Z the old result is 2026-01-15; on a host in America/Los_Angeles the new result is 2026-01-14. sameBillingDay at src/billing/day.ts:8 inherits this: 2026-01-15T23:00:00.000Z and 2026-01-16T01:00:00.000Z were different UTC days (false) and become the same local day in America/New_York (true). Keys already emitted as UTC dates will not match, and two hosts with different TZ settings bucket the same instant onto different days.

findings.title: Keep billingDay on UTC calendar fields
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate and now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which follow the process local timezone. For 2026-01-01T03:00:00.000Z the UTC key is 2026-01-01, but in America/Los_Angeles (UTC-8) the local key is 2025-12-31. sameBillingDay (day.ts:8) then returns false for 2026-01-01T03:00:00.000Z vs 2026-01-01T20:00:00.000Z, which are the same UTC billing day and previously compared equal. The inverse merge happens ahead of UTC (Asia/Tokyo: 2025-12-31T23:00:00.000Z and 2026-01-01T01:00:00.000Z become the same local day). Billing-day keys and same-day checks are therefore host-TZ dependent and disagree with every key produced before this change.

findings.title: Keep billingDay on the UTC calendar date
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay used to format getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, a timezone-stable YYYY-MM-DD. It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which follow the process local zone. The same instant therefore yields a different day string whenever the local offset pushes it across midnight. Example: 2026-03-15T06:30:00.000Z is UTC day 2026-03-15 but America/Los_Angeles day 2026-03-14. sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8) compares those strings, so two instants on one UTC date that straddle local midnight now compare unequal, and any previously stored UTC day key no longer matches.

findings.title: Include tenant in the profile memo key

After readProfile("t1", "acct", fetch) stores t1's Profile, readProfile("t2", "acct", fetch) hits that entry at the `if (cached) return cached` guard and returns t1's tenant and displayName without calling fetchProfile for t2.

After readProfile("acme", "alice", fetch) stores acme's profile, readProfile("globex", "alice", fetch) returns acme's profile and never calls fetchProfile for globex.

findings.title: Include tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile still identifies a profile by (tenant, account) and fetchProfile is still called with both, but the module-level memo now keys only on account. After readProfile("tenant-a", "acct", ...) stores that Profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "acct", ...) takes the cache-hit branch at lines 15-16 and returns tenant-a's Profile (wrong tenant and displayName) without calling fetchProfile. findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors instead of returning ""
findings.whyItBreaks: load still throws Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get returns undefined, then the new bare catch discards that error and returns "". Map<string, string> can already store "", so a missing key and a present empty value are identical. loadAll (keys.map → load) previously aborted the batch on the first missing key; it now returns an array containing "" and continues. The function is exported, so every caller is forced to treat failure as a real string.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: load is exported and previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get(key) was undefined. The new bare catch returns "". Map<string, string> can store "", and a present empty value still returns "" at the line above the catch, so absence and a real empty value are the same result. loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps load over every key; Array.map used to abort the batch when load threw, and it now returns a full string[] with "" in each missing slot. Callers that persist, display, or forward that array treat a failed lookup as stored data. The catch also hides any throw from store.get, not only the missing-key Error.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: load is exported and previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get returned undefined. The new bare catch returns "". A stored empty string is a legitimate Map value and also returns "", so failure and a real empty value are the same result. loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps every key through load and used to abort the whole call when any key was missing; it now returns an array that includes "" for absent keys, which callers persist or report as data that was present.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground failure instead of returning void
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is exported and returns void. The empty catch discards every exception from fn(). The deadline check then returns, and the loop falls off the end with no throw. Success, a thrown fn, a missed deadline, and an exhausted retries count all produce the same undefined return, so a caller cannot avoid treating a failed call as a completed one.

findings.title: Rethrow retryBackground failures instead of returning void
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is exported and declared to return void. If fn throws, the empty catch continues and the function then returns normally once the loop ends. If the deadline has passed, line 23 returns normally as well. Success, every attempt failing, and a timeout are the same normal return, so a caller will persist, bill, or mark complete work that never succeeded.

findings.title: Bound both retry loops with maxAttempts
findings.whyItBreaks: Config.retries (line 3) is a second attempt budget beside the existing maxAttempts. retry loops on config.maxAttempts at line 9 and never reads retries. retryBackground loops on config.retries at line 22 and never reads maxAttempts. The new function is a synchronous copy of retry: it does not schedule work off the caller stack. The same Config {maxAttempts: 5, retries: 1, timeout: 1000} therefore calls fn up to five times from retry and at most once from retryBackground.

findings.title: Rethrow when retryBackground exhausts attempts
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is exported. The empty catch at lines 27-28 discards every exception from fn, the deadline guard at line 23 returns normally after prior failures, and falling out of the loop at line 30 also returns void. That is the same result as the success return at line 26, so a caller cannot tell a completed call from exhaustion or a timeout. No in-repo caller exists; the public void contract still forces every caller to treat failure as success.

findings.title: Numeric values read .length and render len=undefined
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but Field always reads value.length. A number has no length property, so the read is undefined and defaultValue becomes the literal string "len=undefined" (value 42 renders that). String values still produce len=<character count>. The public union promises a number is a valid input; the rendered result for every number is wrong.

findings.title: Stop reading .length on numeric Field values
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported FieldProps.value is string | number, but Field always evaluates value.length. A number has no length property, so the read is undefined and defaultValue becomes the string "len=undefined" (for example value 42). String inputs still render len=<character count>.

findings.title: Compute Field length for numeric values
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported FieldProps.value is string | number (line 2), so a number is a valid argument and the label is what the input receives. value.length exists only on string. For a number it is undefined, and defaultValue becomes the literal "len=undefined" (123, 0, and -12.5 all do this) instead of the character length of that value.

findings.title: Stop echoing the deploy token into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: On every push the new step binds secrets.TOKEN and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN", so the credential is written to step stdout and stored in the Actions log. Log readers are a wider set than people who can read repository secrets, and runner redaction is best-effort: it misses structured values, embedded newlines, and any shell-altered form of the token. The env map applies only to this step, so make build never receives TOKEN; the step's only effect is to emit the secret.

findings.title: Stop printing the deploy token in workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step copies secrets.TOKEN into the step environment and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN". On every push (no branch or environment gate) the shell writes that credential to stdout, which Actions stores in the retained job log. Masking is a later best-effort exact-substring redaction and is unreliable for multiline, split, encoded, or mask-breaking values, so the deploy credential is exposed to anyone who can read Actions logs. The next step, make build, starts a fresh environment and never receives TOKEN, so this step's only effect is that disclosure.

findings.title: Pass merge-base commit as bundle.baseSha
findings.whyItBreaks: bundle.baseSha is now the local baseSha (PR_BASE_SHA, or merge-base of origin/main and HEAD) while patch and changedFiles are still produced from mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha. On the CI path PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip, which is not an ancestor of head whenever the PR is behind that branch, so mergeBase and baseSha differ. review(bundle) then sees a base commit that is not the left side of patch: git diff <bundle.baseSha> <headSha> is a two-dot tree diff that also reverses commits that landed only on the base branch, so the review baseline and the patch describe different changes.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer on git()
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is what captures git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>, the full PR patch. spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1MiB. Above that Node kills the child: status null, signal SIGTERM, error ENOBUFS, stdout truncated (verified on Node v24.15.0 at 1114112 bytes) and stderr empty. status !== 0 therefore throws git diff <sha> <sha> failed: with no reason, and runGithub posts a failed check and sets exitCode 1. The same file still sets maxBuffer to 64MiB for gh and ghText; this drops only the call that emits the largest stdout, so any patch over ~1MiB fails the review.

findings.title: Pass mergeBase as bundle.baseSha so it matches the patch
findings.whyItBreaks: bundle.baseSha is now the raw baseSha (PR_BASE_SHA, else merge-base of origin/main and HEAD) while patch and changedFiles are still taken from mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha). Those commits differ whenever the base tip is not an ancestor of head, which is the normal case when PR_BASE_SHA is GitHub's pull_request.base.sha and the base branch has moved. git diff <bundle.baseSha> <headSha> is then a different change set than patch, so review() is handed a parent tree that is not the left side of the diff it is asked to review. The previous baseSha: mergeBase kept the bundle aligned with the patch.

findings.title: Restore git() 64MiB maxBuffer so large diffs are not killed
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1048576 bytes (verified on Node v24.15.0). git() is what captures the review patch via git diff mergeBase headSha. Stdout of 1048577 bytes returns status null, signal SIGTERM, and error ENOBUFS; res.status !== 0 then throws before review(). The removed option allowed 64MiB, and gh() / ghText() still set that limit. Any patch one byte over 1MiB used to be reviewed and now aborts the check run.

findings.title: Keep bundle.baseSha aligned with the patch merge-base
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub still builds patch with git diff mergeBase headSha (line 140) and changedFiles from that same mergeBase (line 141), but the bundle now stores baseSha (line 165). baseSha is PR_BASE_SHA or merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) (line 138); mergeBase is merge-base(baseSha, headSha) (line 139). On the Actions path PR_BASE_SHA is the live base-branch tip. When that tip is not an ancestor of head, merge-base differs from the tip, so review(bundle) at line 177 receives a base SHA that is not the parent of patch. Re-diffing bundle.baseSha..headSha then includes commits that landed on the base branch after the fork and disagrees with the patch that was actually reviewed.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer so large diffs do not abort
findings.whyItBreaks: git() dropped maxBuffer, so spawnSync uses Node's 1024*1024 default. On Node v24, stdout past that cap kills the child with status null, signal SIGTERM, and error code ENOBUFS. git() treats status !== 0 as failure and throws (line 38), discarding stdout. The full patch is loaded by git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) at line 140, before the try that posts a failed check (line 176). A diff over 1MiB aborts runGithub before review() runs. gh() and ghText() still set maxBuffer to 64MiB, so only git output regressed.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox on codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd set to opts.repoPath and the caller prompt on stdin, and no longer passes `-s read-only`. Codex applies sandbox_mode from CLI flags first, then a trusted project's `.codex/config.toml`, then `~/.codex/config.toml`, and only then the built-in read-only default. Without the flag, a normal workspace-write config (or a trusted checkout whose `.codex/config.toml` sets workspace-write or danger-full-access) is used. In-sandbox writes and local commands run without an approval prompt, so the review agent can create, edit, or delete files in the repository it was only supposed to inspect. The old `-s read-only` argument overrode those layers.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox on codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd opts.repoPath and the prompt on stdin, and CodexOptions has no sandbox field. Without `-s`, codex 0.155 leaves the sandbox override unset (exec/src/lib.rs:328-331 and ConfigOverrides.sandbox_mode at :570) and forces approval_policy=never (:568); exec mode also rejects permission-approval requests. derive_permission_profile then uses sandbox_mode_override.or(config.sandbox_mode) (config_toml.rs:758 on rust-v0.155.0, which 0.155.1 only hotfixes for TUI reasoning summaries). ~/.codex/config.toml:1 is sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" and does not set default_permissions, so the model gets unsandboxed filesystem and network access with no prompt. The removed `-s read-only` was the CLI override that beat that config. Prompt text is untrusted review input, so the agent can write the target repo or run arbitrary commands.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox on codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex is the exported spawn path and CodexOptions has no sandbox field, so the hardcoded -s read-only was the only pin. spawnSync still sets cwd to opts.repoPath and passes the prompt on stdin. Without -s, Codex resolves sandbox_mode from a trusted project's .codex/config.toml, then ~/.codex/config.toml, then the built-in default (CLI flag > project config > user config > built-in). The exec built-in default is read-only, but the usual local setting sandbox_mode=workspace-write, and danger-full-access, now apply. codex exec does not stop for in-boundary approval, so the model can edit opts.repoPath and run workspace commands; danger-full-access also drops the filesystem and network boundary. Previously -s read-only overrode that config.

findings.title: Diff merge-base against headSha, not baseSha against HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub now sets the review patch with `git diff baseSha HEAD` and passes that same baseSha into changedFileSet, which runs `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` (line 57). baseSha is PR_BASE_SHA when that variable is set, i.e. the base branch tip. The removed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` was what restricted the diff to the fork point. On a PR that is behind its base, the two-dot diff treats commits that landed only on the base as PR changes (a file added only on the base appears as a deletion) and omits PR edits whose blob now matches the base tip. The patch also ends at the literal checkout HEAD, while bundle.headSha (line 165) and the GitHub review commit_id in postReview (line 85) stay on PR_HEAD_SHA whenever that env var differs from HEAD. Inline comments are then positioned against a different tree than the commit the review API receives; GitHub rejects the payload, and the catch at line 96 republishes the review with every inline comment removed. changedPaths is built from that file list, so the inlineComments filter (line 63) keeps findings for paths outside the PR's three-dot diff. With both env vars unset, baseSha is already merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) and headSha is HEAD, and the old second merge-base was idempotent — the regression is the env-var path this Actions entrypoint is written to honor.

findings.title: Use merge-base..headSha for the review patch
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub still records headSha from PR_HEAD_SHA (or rev-parse HEAD) and posts the review commit_id and the check-run head_sha on that value, but the patch is now `git diff baseSha HEAD` and changedFileSet is called with baseSha. PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip. When that tip has commits the PR head does not contain, the two-dot diff reports those base-only commits as PR deletions and substitutes the net tip-to-tip tree difference for the PR's own delta. The same pair feeds changedPaths, so inline comments follow that wrong file set. When Actions checks out the pull_request merge ref, HEAD and PR_HEAD_SHA are different commits, so the verdict is attached to a SHA whose tree was not diffed. With both env vars unset, baseSha is already merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) and headSha is HEAD, so that fallback path is unchanged; the regression is the env-provided range.

findings.title: Restore merge-base..headSha as the review diff
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub still resolves headSha from PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137) and posts both the review and the check run on that SHA (commit_id at line 85, head_sha at line 124). The patch and the changed-file set are now `git diff <baseSha> HEAD` (lines 139-140; changedFileSet repeats that range at line 57). PR_BASE_SHA replaces the merge-base fallback and is the base-branch tip on the Actions path this function requires (pull_request.base.sha). That two-dot diff treats every base-only commit after the fork as a PR edit, and it drops a file the PR changed when the base tip has the same final blob. changedPaths (line 141) then keeps or drops inline comments against that wrong set (line 63), and the model reviews base-branch edits as the pull request. The diff end is the literal HEAD, so when PR_HEAD_SHA is set and the pull_request checkout is the synthetic merge commit, comment lines come from a different tree than commit_id. GitHub rejects that review payload and the catch at lines 96-109 retries with every inline comment removed. git merge-base used to exit non-zero when the two SHAs do not share an ancestor, git() threw, and the catch at lines 181-192 failed the check; git diff exits 0 for that same pair and the run can report pass on a full-tree patch.

findings.title: Keep replace replacers as functions so $ sequences stay literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $$, $&, $`, and $' in a string replacement (ECMAScript GetSubstitution) and inserts the result unchanged only when the replacement is a function. The previous () => value replacers existed for that reason. JSON.stringify does not escape $, and bundle.patch is a diff. A patch or finding containing bash $'...', $$, or $& is rewritten before runCodex: $$ becomes $, $& becomes the placeholder text ({{BUNDLE}}, {{FINDINGS}}, or {{PATCH}}), $` inserts the prompt prefix, and $' splices the rest of the prompt into the inserted body. The review and critic models then judge a different diff than the PR.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so dollar sequences stay literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace runs GetSubstitution on a string replacement: $$ becomes $, $& becomes the matched placeholder, $` becomes the prompt text before the placeholder, and $' becomes the text after it. A function replacement inserts its return value literally, which is what the previous code did. JSON.stringify does not escape $, and bundle.patch is raw diff text, so ordinary Make, shell, and regex snippets ($$, $&, $', $`) are rewritten before runCodex sees them at lines 28 and 34. On the critic path the damage compounds: a $' inside the findings JSON expands to the remainder of critic.md, which still contains {{PATCH}}; the next replace substitutes only the first {{PATCH}}, so the patch is written into the findings section and the real patch slot can stay unfilled. deriveVerdict and the returned ReviewResult (lines 37-44) are built from that critic output, so the published review describes a different diff than bundle.patch.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so $ in diffs stays literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement runs ECMA-262 GetSubstitution even when the search value is a plain string and there are no capture groups: $$ becomes $, $& becomes the matched token ({{BUNDLE}}/{{FINDINGS}}/{{PATCH}}), $` inserts the entire prompt prefix, and $' inserts the entire prompt suffix. The previous () => value replacers inserted text verbatim. JSON.stringify does not escape $, and bundle.patch is raw diff text, so ordinary diffs corrupt the prompt before runCodex: a Makefile/shell/template `$$` is reviewed as a single `$` (e.g. `$${amount}` becomes `${amount}`), and a bash ANSI-C `$'` or a `$`+backtick splices the rest of critic.md or review.md into the patch or the JSON, changing what the critic compares and often making the embedded JSON invalid. Same rewrite hits {{FINDINGS}} when a finding quotes those sequences.

findings.title: Pin the fallback review to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview's catch path runs when the JSON review (inline comments plus commit_id) is rejected, then submits only event and body. GitHub's create-review API treats an omitted commit_id as the pull request's most recent commit. runGithub passes the SHA it actually reviewed (PR_HEAD_SHA, or git rev-parse HEAD) into postReview and postCheck records the verdict on that same SHA. Those SHAs differ when the head moves during await review(), on a re-run of an older workflow SHA, or when PR_HEAD_SHA is pinned while GitHub's head has advanced — the same situations that 422 the commented review and force this fallback. The fallback then submits COMMENT, or REQUEST_CHANGES when the verdict is changes_requested, against a commit Needlefish did not review, while the check run stays on the reviewed SHA.

findings.title: Pin the fallback review to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the commented review POST throws, the catch retries with only event and body. GitHub's create-review API defaults an omitted commit_id to the pull request's most recent commit. headSha is captured at line 141 and the diff is taken against it at line 144, before await review() at line 181, so a push during the review makes that latest commit a different SHA. COMMENT and REQUEST_CHANGES are then stored against code this run did not review, while postCheck at line 184 still publishes the check on the original headSha.

findings.title: Stop turning malformed findings into real P1 bugs
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to throw on a non-object, an unknown severity or category, an empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a non-finite or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd. Those throws reached normalizeReview: strict=true (the default) propagated the error, and strict=false dropped that finding. The throws are gone and strict is gone, so normalizeReview at line 131 now keeps every element. An empty object becomes severity P1 (a real SEVERITIES member), category bug, title "Untitled finding", file "", lineStart 0, lineEnd 0, and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix. Number("n/a") is NaN, which JSON.stringify emits as null. Callers cannot tell a parse failure from a model that reported a P1, and normalizeReview(raw, false) no longer drops bad entries because the second argument is ignored. A null element still throws TypeError, so the same array both fabricates findings and crashes.

findings.title: Trim category and file before coercing them
findings.whyItBreaks: Severity is still trim+uppercase before the allow-list check, but category is tested raw. The previous normalizer did String(raw.category ?? "").trim(), so category " security " was kept as security. CATEGORIES.includes(" security ") is false, and the else branch stores "bug", so a security finding is relabeled bug and then returned by normalizeReview at line 131. File is no longer trimmed either: " src/a.ts " is returned with the spaces, so it no longer matches the path the old normalizer emitted.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of synthesizing P1 bugs
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on a non-object, an unknown severity or category, an empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a non-finite or non-positive line (base src/shared/schema.ts:96-121). Those throws reached normalizeReview, which either failed the review (strict default) or dropped the bad element (strict=false, base src/shared/schema.ts:155-165). The new body never throws for those cases: an unknown severity becomes "P1" (line 98), a missing title becomes "Untitled finding" (line 99), an unknown category becomes "bug" (lines 100-102), and file, lineStart, lineEnd, whyItBreaks, and suggestedFix become "" or 0 (lines 103-108). Non-finite input such as lineStart "n/a" is stored as NaN because Number() is no longer passed through Number.isFinite. Category and file are no longer trimmed, so a previously accepted category like "security " is relabeled "bug". normalizeReview dropped the strict parameter and now always does raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) (line 131), so the fabricated Finding is saved on RawReview. Failure and a real P1 bug are indistinguishable, and a review that used to fail parsing now succeeds with a blocking invented finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of inventing P1s
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to throw on a non-object, an unknown severity or category, a blank file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or a non-finite lineStart/lineEnd <= 0. It now always returns a Finding: unknown severity becomes "P1" (line 98), unknown category becomes "bug" (lines 100-102), missing file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become "" (lines 103, 107-108), and missing lines become 0 (lines 104-105). Non-numeric lines become NaN because `?? 0` does not replace them and there is no Number.isFinite check; JSON.stringify turns NaN/Infinity into null. normalizeReview (line 131) is the public parser and previously defaulted to strict=true, so one bad element failed the whole call with no RawReview. It now maps every element through the coercer and returns those objects as findings (lines 136-141). `{summary, findings:[{}], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}` used to throw `malformed finding: invalid severity ""`; it now succeeds as a P1/bug "Untitled finding" at file "" lines 0-0, indistinguishable from a real P1. The deleted strict=false path dropped bad elements; the second argument is now ignored, so they are inserted instead. A review that mixes one valid finding with one empty object used to produce nothing (strict) or only the valid finding (non-strict); it now publishes the fabricated P1 alongside the real one.

findings.title: Pass repository to gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch has no pull_request payload, so EVENT_HEAD is empty and the else branch is the live path (job if at line 24 still runs the job). That branch runs before actions/checkout. gh pr view with no -R/--repo and no GH_REPO resolves the repo only from git remotes in the working directory; it does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (cli/cli still tracks this as open issue 3556; BaseRepoFunc returns the remotes error). On a clean or ephemeral self-hosted workspace there is no .git, so gh exits non-zero and the Resolve PR refs step fails under the default bash -e, and the manual review never checks out the PR. A leftover or parent git checkout binds the lookup to that remote instead of github.repository, so PR numbers are resolved in the wrong repo.

findings.title: Pin gh pr view to this repo before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: These lines run only on workflow_dispatch (EVENT_HEAD is empty because there is no pull_request payload) and they run before actions/checkout. gh 2.98 resolves a repo only from -R or GH_REPO, then from git remotes; it does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (cli/cli pkg/cmdutil/repo_override.go OverrideBaseRepoFunc). Removing -R "$REPO" leaves neither, so in a clean workspace gh exits with "not a git repository". The exit status is discarded by $(...) — bash -eo pipefail still continues, verified with bash 5.2 — so GITHUB_OUTPUT receives head= and base=. actions/checkout@v4 treats an empty ref as unset (input-helper.ts: if (!result.ref) use github.context.ref and github.context.sha). For workflow_dispatch that is the branch selected in "Use workflow from", not the PR head. The review step then runs that tree with empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA while holding pull-requests: write.

findings.title: Restore -R on pre-checkout gh pr view
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the workflow_dispatch path (EVENT_HEAD is github.event.pull_request.head.sha, empty on dispatch). It runs before checkout, and this diff drops REPO/-R. gh does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (only -R, GH_REPO, or a local remote); in a non-git directory `gh pr view` exits 1 with `fatal: not a git repository` and empty stdout. The default Actions shell is `bash -eo pipefail`, but `echo "head=$(gh ...)"` does not abort: the failure is discarded and GITHUB_OUTPUT gets head= and base=. actions/checkout@v4 treats an empty ref as unset (input-helper.ts: if (!result.ref) use github.context.ref and github.context.sha), so the job checks out the dispatch branch instead of the PR head and runs the review with empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA.

findings.title: Restore throws for malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported normalizeReview used to throw Error("malformed review output: ...") when raw was null/non-object or when summary was not a string or findings, checked, or residual_risks was not an array (base src/shared/schema.ts:115-131). Those branches now substitute "", [], [], and []. normalizeReview(null) and normalizeReview({summary:"",findings:[],checked:[],residual_risks:[]}) therefore return the same RawReview, so parse failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings. A non-array residual_risks, including a single {text, blocks:true} object, becomes [] while summary and findings are still returned, so a blocking risk is dropped and the result looks complete.

findings.title: Reject malformed reviews instead of returning an empty one
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported normalizeReview previously threw Error("malformed review output: ...") when raw was not an object, summary was not a string, or findings/checked/residual_risks was not an array (base src/shared/schema.ts:115-130). Those throws are removed. null, a prose string, {}, or {summary:"ok"} now return a RawReview with missing arrays replaced by [] and summary coerced via String(raw?.summary ?? ""). That is the same value a legitimate zero-finding review already produced and was accepted ({summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}). A dropped or non-array findings payload is therefore reported as no findings. Nothing in the repo calls this function; the public return value forces every caller to treat failure as a real empty review.

findings.title: Propagate malformed review errors instead of empty defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported. At base 2acf679 it threw Error before returning when raw was null/non-object (schema.ts:115), summary was not a string (:118), or findings/checked/residual_risks was not an array (:121, :124, :127). Those throws are gone. null, a non-object, or an object whose findings or residual_risks is missing or not an array now returns {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} (or that shape with a coerced summary), which is identical to a well-formed review that found nothing and has no blocking residual risk. A non-array residual_risks payload is dropped rather than rejected, so a blocks signal that failed to parse cannot fail the review. There is no in-repo caller (only the definition at schema.ts:114); every caller of this public function is forced to treat parse failure as a successful empty review.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution on workflow_dispatch

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer so large diffs do not abort
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync’s default maxBuffer is 1024*1024. On Node v24.15.0, stdout past that limit kills the child (status null, signal SIGTERM, error ENOBUFS). git() only checks res.status !== 0, so it throws `git diff <base> HEAD failed:` with an empty stderr and never returns the patch. runLocal calls git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) for the entire review diff and does not catch that throw, so any patch between 1MiB and the previous 64MiB cap aborts before review(). The adjacent gh() helper still sets maxBuffer to 64MiB.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer so diffs over 1MiB still review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync now omits maxBuffer, so Node 24 uses the 1MiB default (1048576 bytes succeeds; 1048577 bytes returns status null, signal SIGTERM, error ENOBUFS). git() treats status !== 0 as fatal and runLocal does not catch it. The full patch fetch at runLocal, git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]), previously succeeded up to the explicit 64MiB cap (still used by gh() at line 36). Any unified diff over 1MiB now throws `git diff … failed:` with empty stderr, because res.error is not included, and review never runs.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer so diffs over 1MiB still review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1MiB. On Node v24.15.0, a stdout write of 1024*1024+10 bytes returns status null, signal SIGTERM, and error code ENOBUFS. git() treats status !== 0 as fatal, and runLocal calls git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) with no try/catch, so any patch over 1MiB — previously allowed up to 64MiB — aborts the review. stderr is empty on this kill, so the thrown text is only "git diff <base> HEAD failed:". The adjacent gh() helper still sets maxBuffer to 64MiB.

findings.title: Fail the Needlefish check when review throws
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path used to post conclusion "failure" and still tells GitHub "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." It now posts "neutral". GitHub treats neutral as a successful conclusion for required status checks and for dependent checks, same as success and skipped. This adapter does not fail the process on a changes_requested verdict (exit stays 0 after line 184); merge blocking for that verdict is only the Needlefish check conclusion. After this change a thrown review satisfies that required check, and the conclusion is identical to needs_human, so branch protection can no longer tell a crashed review from a non-blocking one. process.exitCode = 1 still fails the Actions job, but that job is not how a failing verdict blocks.
