findings.title: Restore severity canonicalization; stop defaulting it to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously did String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() and only then checked SEVERITIES, defaulting a true miss to P1. The new check is SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) with strict equality against "P0"|"P1"|"P2"|"P3", else "P3". Inputs that used to canonicalize now miss and are stored as P3: "p0" was P0 and is now P3; " P1 " and "p1" were P1 and are now P3; "p2" was P2 and is now P3. Missing, blank, and unrecognized values (undefined, "", "critical") moved from P1 to P3. normalizeReview maps every raw finding through this helper and returns the result with no second severity check, so a high-severity label is indistinguishable from an author-supplied P3. Sibling malformed fields in normalizeReview throw; this path accepts the failure and publishes it as a real lowest-severity finding.

findings.title: Canonical severities fall through and are stored as P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding used to set sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() and accept sev when it was in SEVERITIES (P0–P3), else P1. The new predicate is SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) with no trim or case fold, and the miss path is "P3". Substitution on the live caller normalizeReview (raw findings are any JSON, schema.ts:132): severity "p0" → includes false @97 → "P3" (was "P0"); " P1 " and "p2\n" likewise become "P3" (were "P1"/"P2"). A highest-priority finding is persisted and returned as the lowest priority. Exact "P0"–"P3" still pass.

findings.title: Do not downgrade non-canonical severities to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview (schema.ts:132) feeds untyped model JSON through exported normalizeFinding and returns the result with no second severity check. The allow-list is now exact === against ["P0","P1","P2","P3"]. Substituting the values the deleted String().trim().toUpperCase() path accepted: severity "p0" fails includes and is stored as "P3" (base stored "P0"); " P1 " and "p2" likewise become "P3" (base "P1"/"P2"); omitted severity becomes "P3" (base "P1"). "P3" is also a legal author-supplied severity, so a parse failure and a real low-severity finding are the same value on the public Finding. A P0/P1 issue therefore leaves this function labeled P3.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrub before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex launches `codex exec` against opts.repoPath. The previous revision copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawn. spawnSync with no env option inherits the parent environment (Node child_process default; confirmed: an omitted env forwards all three values, and the same spawn with those keys deleted forwards none). The read-only sandbox flag does not clear the environment, so the agent and any gh/git helper it runs authenticate as the parent, and the tokens can be written into the last-message text this function returns.

findings.title: Stop leaking GitHub tokens into the codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync is called with no env option, so Node's default applies and the child inherits process.env. The parent revision copied the environment and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before the spawn. runCodex passes a caller-supplied prompt to `codex exec -s read-only` and returns the agent's last-message file verbatim, so those credentials are now in the agent process and can be written back out through that file. CI parents routinely have GITHUB_TOKEN set.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token stripping before the codex spawn
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync is invoked with no env option. Node v24.15.0 normalizeSpawnArguments (lib/child_process.js:684) sets the child environment to options.env || { ...process.env }, so codex exec now receives GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN whenever the parent has them. The previous revision cloned process.env, deleted those three names, and passed that object as env. runCodex is exported, feeds a caller-supplied prompt on stdin, sets cwd to opts.repoPath, and returns the child's last message or stdout, so those credentials sit in an agent process that reads attacker-controlled repo content and can copy them into the returned output or the model request. The -s read-only argument leaves the process environment in place.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard on the self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: on.pull_request (opened/synchronize/reopened) starts job review on runs-on: self-hosted. The removed if was the only check that github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name equals github.repository, so a fork PR was skipped. With it gone the job always checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha, then runs pnpm install --frozen-lockfile and ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts from that commit under shell: zsh -l. Fork-controlled lifecycle scripts and src/cli.ts therefore execute as the runner user and can persist on a self-hosted machine for later trusted jobs. Fork pull_request still withholds repo secrets and forces GITHUB_TOKEN read-only, but that does not stop host execution. Maintainer workflow approval does not bring this guard back: once the run is approved, these steps still run.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard on the self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: The review job is on: pull_request and runs-on: self-hosted. It checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha, then runs pnpm install and ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts from that tree under a login shell, with GH_TOKEN set. The deleted if (github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository) was the only condition that skipped this job for fork PRs. After merge, a fork pull_request no longer skips: the fork commit's install scripts and src/cli.ts execute on the persistent self-hosted runner. Fork pull_request runs do not receive Actions secrets and GITHUB_TOKEN stays read-only, but the runner is not an ephemeral VM, so that code can persist and steal secrets or write tokens from later trusted jobs on the same machine.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard on the self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: The review job triggers on pull_request (opened, synchronize, reopened) and the same-repo if was the only gate. It runs on self-hosted, checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha (line 23), then under zsh -l runs pnpm install --frozen-lockfile (line 28, lifecycle scripts from the PR manifest) and ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts with GH_TOKEN set (line 34). For a fork that head SHA is untrusted. Previously the job ran only when github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository, so fork heads were skipped. Same-repo PRs already passed that check; this deletion only adds fork execution. Fork pull_request runs do not receive repository secrets and GitHub forces GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only, but the runner is persistent and the login shell is a long-lived user, so code from the fork runs on that host and can poison later trusted jobs.

findings.title: Honor explicit zero runner kill delays
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs now returns fallbackMs when the parsed duration is 0. NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 therefore becomes 5000, and the timer at line 124 waits 5000ms after SIGTERM before SIGKILL. NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 becomes 2000, and the timer at line 123 waits 2000ms before finish() resolves a child that never emits close. A configured zero is a real delay (the next timer turn) and is now indistinguishable from an unset variable, so a hung runner cannot be reaped without those default waits.

findings.title: Honor explicit zero grace and give-up delays
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs used to return a finite parsed duration of 0. The new `parsed > 0` check rejects it and returns fallbackMs. Both live readers are kill timers: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (fallback 5000 at lines 3-6) is passed to setTimeout at line 124, so SIGKILL waits 5000ms after SIGTERM instead of being armed immediately; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 (fallback 2000 at lines 7-10) is passed to setTimeout at line 123, so finish() waits 2000ms after SIGKILL instead of unblocking on the next tick. A timed-out child that ignores SIGTERM keeps running for the default grace, and a setsid-escaped descendant holds the spawn promise for the default give-up. Empty, non-numeric, and negative inputs already used the fallback; only explicit zero changed.

findings.title: Accept explicit 0ms runner kill delays
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs now requires parsed > 0, so the string "0" (also "0.0", "+0", "-0") takes the fallback branch. At import, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 therefore becomes 5000 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 becomes 2000. Those constants are the delays at setTimeout (lines 124 and 123) with no later clamp. Node 24 accepts setTimeout(..., 0) and schedules it at 1ms (_idleTimeout 1); it does not reject 0. An operator who set grace to 0 to SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM now waits 5000ms, and one who set give-up to 0 to stop waiting for "close" now waits 2000ms. Explicit zero is indistinguishable from unset or garbage.

findings.title: Restore tail coverage so capped hotspots cannot skip changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge keeps only sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) (MAX_HOTSPOTS is 6 at line 26). The tail hotspot that appended every changed path missing from that set is gone, so the loop at line 97 deep-reviews only those hotspots. isLarge (line 30) sends every bundle with more than 10 changed files or a patch longer than 30000 characters here. A map that returns 7 or more hotspots, or that omits a changed path from the top 6, never passes those paths to runCodex. The critic is given only patchStat (line 117), so it cannot read the skipped diffs. deriveVerdict (line 122) then scores the reviewed subset, and a clean subset is returned as the whole review.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks instead of hardcoding []
findings.whyItBreaks: A successful deep pass returns residual_risks that can carry blocks:true when a gap must stop a pass. The loop keeps only res.findings (lines 103-105) and candidateMerged.residual_risks is fixed to []. That object is the critic FINDINGS payload (line 116). deriveVerdict (line 122) and the returned residualRisks (line 128) come from the critic output, which never received those entries. A deep pass with no findings and a blocking residual is therefore serialized as an empty non-blocking review, and the large-PR result can pass. Previously this array was the accumulated deep-pass residuals (base src/core/review.ts:127 and :140) that the critic prompt received (base :143).

findings.title: Put whyItBreaks back on the dedup key

Two findings that share those fields and describe different failures collide. On equal severity line 39 keeps the first and drops the second, so the second defect never reaches the critic. reviewLarge concatenates every hotspot's findings and dedups them at line 108, and overlapping hotspots routinely emit same-line findings whose titles match while whyItBreaks differs. The previous key included norm(whyItBreaks).slice(0, 80) (base src/core/review.ts:38), so those two findings both survived.

A deep pass that returns blocks:true is therefore serialized as an empty list, which is the same input as a clean pass. findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge runs whenever patch length > 30000 or changedFiles.length > 10, then keeps only sortByRisk(...).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) (6) and deep-reviews that list. The deleted backstop pushed every changed path absent from those hotspots into a tail hotspot. findings.title: Forward deep-pass blocking residuals instead of []

A deep pass that returns blocks:true is sent to the critic as an empty list, the same payload as a clean review, so deriveVerdict (line 122) and the returned residualRisks (line 128) cannot see that block. "(none)" for {{FOCUS}} is gone, and the head file never reads bundle.focus. Math.round half-up turns a remainder of 59500–59999 ms into 60, and nothing carries that into minutes. 119500 ms becomes minutes=1 and seconds=60, so the stats line is "1m 60s" (nearest second is 2m 0s). findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function name and the error at line 33 promise a positive integer, but `parsed < 0` now lets every integer that is not strictly negative through. Number("0"), Number("-0"), Number(""), Number(" "), and Number("0.0") are all integers and fail `parsed < 0`, so the function returns 0 or -0 instead of throwing. Callers of this public parser cannot tell a rejected non-positive value from a successful parse, and a returned -0 yields -Infinity under reciprocal use.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger to honor its contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger is exported and still promises a positive integer (name at line 30; throw text "requires a positive integer" at line 33). The guard changed from parsed <= 0 to parsed < 0, so a numeric zero no longer throws and is returned as a successful value. Number("0"), Number("-0"), Number(""), and Number(" ") are all 0 or -0; Number.isInteger is true for those and -0 < 0 is false, so "0", "-0", "", and whitespace now return 0/-0. Previously the same inputs threw. Callers cannot tell invalid non-positive input from a real result, and a returned 0 is not a positive integer.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger is exported and its throw text still says the label "requires a positive integer", so the contract is an integer greater than 0 or an error.
